title: Words at work
grammar: Word formation for B2 (noun/adjective/adverb suffixes, negative prefixes)

scene.speaker: nova
scene.bubble: Words are tools too! Meet the language of work, learn how English builds word families, and master the word-formation task.
scene.intro: Welcome to Unit 3. Our Trades project turns to the language of work itself. In this unit you read how English builds whole families of words from a single root, you learn the suffixes and prefixes that make nouns, adjectives and adverbs, and you practise the word-formation task from Reading and Use of English Part 3. One root, many words — let's build them together.

activities.title: Reading — how English builds a career

data.title: How English builds a career
data.author: nadia
data.text:
As part of Inspiring Nordic, our class interviewed local workers about their jobs. What fascinated me was not only what they do, but the language they use — because English builds so many work words from a single root.

Take the verb employ. Add a suffix and you get employment; add a prefix and you get unemployment; change it again and you describe an employer and an employee. One small word grows into a whole family.

Sofía interviewed a nurse who spoke about responsibility, patience and reliability — all nouns formed from adjectives and verbs. Mateo met an electrician who valued qualifications and expertise above everything.

The pattern is powerful. If you know the suffixes, you can guess new words. The ending -ment often makes a noun; -able makes an adjective; -ly makes an adverb; and prefixes like un-, in- or dis- reverse a meaning. That is exactly what the Cambridge exam tests in the word-formation task.

Liam put it well: “Learning one root is like getting several words for free.” He is right. The more you notice how words are built, the more professional and confident your English becomes — at work and in the exam.

data.title: Word formation for B2
data.intro: In word formation you change the form of a root word — usually by adding a suffix or prefix — so that it fits the gap. Common changes make nouns, adjectives, adverbs, or opposites.
rules: Suffixes often change word class: -ment/-tion/-ity make nouns, -able/-ful/-ive make adjectives, -ly makes adverbs.
Negative prefixes like un-, in-, im-, dis- reverse the meaning (happy → unhappy).
Read the whole sentence: decide the word class and whether it is positive, negative, singular or plural.

activities.title: Listening — the word-formation task. Write ONE word in each gap.

data.voice_note: Voz: la profesora (Miss Vega), sobre la tarea de formación de palabras.
data.script: Hello, Grade 10. Today we focus on word formation, which appears in Part three of the exam. Remember three simple tricks. First, decide the word class you need: a noun, an adjective, or an adverb. Second, watch for negative prefixes; sometimes the answer must be negative, like unemployment. Third, check whether the noun should be plural. For homework, choose one root, such as employ, and build a whole family of words around it. Nadia will collect your lists on Friday. Work carefully, and your vocabulary will grow quickly.

activities.title: Speaking — skills and word families. In pairs, then record it.

data.text: In pairs, talk about skills and jobs. Model: “A good nurse needs patience, reliability and real expertise.” 1) Which three qualities make someone employable, and why? 2) Turn each quality into a noun, an adjective and an adverb (e.g. create → creativity → creative → creatively). 3) Which job in your town do people most admire, and what skills does it need? Give reasons and examples, then record your discussion.

homework.prompt: Choose four root words connected with work (e.g. employ, create, rely, profession). For each, write two sentences using different formed words — a noun, an adjective, an adverb or a negative form. Aim for 8–10 sentences in total. Capital letters and full stops!
